current_example.title: Example: Simplifying a Radical Expression That Is Not a Perfect Square With Domain Restrictions

q-141778.name: Question 1
q-141778.worked_solution:
We first write $25{r}^{3}$ as the product $25{r}^{2}\cdot r$ which contains a perfect square $(25{r}^{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{25{r}^{3}} & = \\ \sqrt{25{r}^{2}\cdot r} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{25{r}^{2}\cdot r} & = \\ \sqrt{(5r)^{2}\cdot r} & = \\ \sqrt{(5r)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{r} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(5r)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{r} & = \\ |5r|\cdot \sqrt{r} & = \\ |5|\cdot |r|\cdot \sqrt{r} & = \\ 5|r|\sqrt{r} & \end{aligned}
$$

q-141778.html:
Question 1
?

Simplify 25r3.

a
5|r|5r
b
5r2r
c
5|r|r
d
|r|5r
e
5r25r
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first write 25r3 as the product 25r2⋅r which contains a perfect square (25r2):

25r3=25r2⋅r

Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals:

25r2⋅r=(5r)2⋅r=(5r)2⋅r

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

(5r)2⋅r=|5r|⋅r=|5|⋅|r|⋅r=5|r|r

q-141464.name: Question 2
q-141464.worked_solution:
We first write $54{y}^{2}$ as the product $9{y}^{2}\cdot 6$ which contains a perfect square $(9{y}^{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{54{y}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{9{y}^{2}\cdot 6} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9{y}^{2}\cdot 6} & = \\ \sqrt{(3y)^{2}\cdot 6} & = \\ \sqrt{(3y)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{6} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(3y)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{6} & = \\ |3y|\cdot \sqrt{6} & = \\ |3|\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{6} & = \\ 3|y|\sqrt{6} & \end{aligned}
$$

q-142029.name: Question 3
q-142029.worked_solution:
We first write $144{b}^{7}$ as the product $144{b}^{6}\cdot b$ which contains a perfect square $(144{b}^{6}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{144{b}^{7}} & = \\ \sqrt{144{b}^{6}\cdot b} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{144{b}^{6}\cdot b} & = \\ \sqrt{{(12{b}^{3})}^{2}\cdot b} & = \\ \sqrt{{(12{b}^{3})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{b} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(12{b}^{3})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{b} & = \\ |12{b}^{3}|\cdot \sqrt{b} & = \\ |12|\cdot |{b}^{3}|\cdot \sqrt{b} & = \\ 12|b{|}^{3}\sqrt{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify 144b7.

a
|b|34b
b
12|b|3b
c
6|b|32b
d
|b|33b
e
6|b|2b
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first write 144b7 as the product 144b6⋅b which contains a perfect square (144b6):

144b7=144b6⋅b

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals:

144b6⋅b=(12b3)2⋅b=(12b3)2⋅b

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

(12b3)2⋅b=|12b3|⋅b=|12|⋅|b3|⋅b=12|b|3b

q-141477.name: Question 4
q-141477.worked_solution:
We first write $44{u}^{8}$ as the product $4{u}^{8}\cdot 11$ which contains a perfect square $(4{u}^{8}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{44{u}^{8}} & = \\ \sqrt{4{u}^{8}\cdot 11} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4{u}^{8}\cdot 11} & = \\ \sqrt{{(2{u}^{4})}^{2}\cdot 11} & = \\ \sqrt{{(2{u}^{4})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{11} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(2{u}^{4})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{11} & = \\ |2{u}^{4}|\cdot \sqrt{11} & = \\ |2|\cdot |{u}^{4}|\cdot \sqrt{11} & = \\ 2|u{|}^{4}\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

q-2934.name: Question 5
q-2934.worked_solution:
We first write $8{a}^{2}$ as the product $4{a}^{2}\cdot 2$ which contains a perfect square $(4{a}^{2}).$ Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{8{a}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{4{a}^{2}\cdot 2} & = \\ \sqrt{(2a)^{2}\cdot 2} & = \\ \sqrt{(2a)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ |2a|\sqrt{2} & = \\ |2|\cdot |a|\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ 2\cdot |a|\cdot \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a\ge 0,$ we have $|a|=a,$ and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |a|\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ 2\cdot a\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ 2a\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-3052.name: Question 6
q-3052.worked_solution:
We first write $32{y}^{3}$ as the product $16{y}^{2}\cdot 2y$ which contains a perfect square $(16{y}^{2}).$ Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{32{y}^{3}} & = \\ \sqrt{16{y}^{2}\cdot 2y} & = \\ \sqrt{(4y)^{2}\cdot 2y} & = \\ \sqrt{(4y)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ |4y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ |4|\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ we have $|y|=y,$ and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4\cdot y\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4y\sqrt{2y}.\end{aligned}

q-3052.html:
Question 6
?

Simplify 32y3 given that y≥0.

a
8y2y
b
4y4y
c
2y28y
d
4y2y
e
2y8y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first write 32y3 as the product 16y2⋅2y which contains a perfect square (16y2). Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified: 32y3=16y2⋅2y=(4y)2⋅2y=(4y)2⋅2y=|4y|⋅2y=|4|⋅|y|⋅2y=4⋅|y|⋅2y

Since y≥0, we have |y|=y, and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is 4⋅|y|⋅2y=4⋅y⋅2y=4y2y.
